Each rung answers three mandatory questions:

\paragraph{Rung 1: Primitive
Difference}\label{rung-1-primitive-difference}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?} The primitive difference operator
  \(D(x, y) := y - x\) on discrete carrier coordinates, certified
  sameness (\(x \sim y \iff D(x, y) = 0\)), antisymmetry
  (\(D(x, y) = -D(y, x)\)), and the 1-cocycle identity on 0-simplexes
  (\(D(x, y) + D(y, z) = D(x, z)\)). Mechanized in
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  (\texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}f},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}q},
  \texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}m},
  \texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e})
  and computed in
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}.
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} A
  declared discrete carrier set equipped with an abelian subtraction
  operation (integer coordinates \(\mathbb{Z}\)). No metric, topology,
  probabilities, or Hilbert space are imported.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What is not selected by these data?} The declared
  difference and equality relation do not select the norm, topology, or
  physical geometry required by the later quantum models. Those
  structures must be specified separately. For example, the same
  equality relation already defines the discrete metric \(d_D(x,y)=0\)
  when \(D(x,y)=0\) and \(d_D(x,y)=1\) otherwise, so the issue is
  nonselection of the intended geometry, not impossibility of defining
  any metric. A finite discrete state set admits no nontrivial
  continuous action of the connected translation group; a finite set of
  basis labels does not prevent continuous transformations of amplitudes
  over a supplied scalar field.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Rung 2: Finite Cochain
Packet}\label{rung-2-finite-cochain-packet}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?} The coboundary sequence
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle C^0 \xrightarrow{d_0} C^1 \xrightarrow{d_1} C^2\)}\]
  on a declared directed 2-complex, boundary nilpotence \(d_1 d_0 = 0\),
  a finite linear-program formulation of quotient mass
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \Phi_1([x]) = \inf_\alpha \|x - d_0 \alpha\|_{1, w}\)}\],
  the gauge-invariant closure defect \(\Gamma_2([x]) = \|d_1 x\|_1\),
  and the diagnostic trichotomy
  (\texttt{E\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s},
  \texttt{C\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}R\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l},
  \texttt{A\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e}).
  Mechanized in
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  (\texttt{d\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o},
  \texttt{c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{d\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}y},
  \texttt{n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}y})
  and computed in
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
  and
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}.
  The cochain Python implementation uses floating-point HiGHS with
  tolerance \(10^{-9}\); it does not certify exact zero or exact LP
  optimality. The cited Lean declarations prove algebraic identities,
  not correctness of that solver.
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} A
  declared finite directed 2-complex (vertices, directed edges, oriented
  2-cells) and positive edge weights \(w_e > 0\).
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?} Non-trivial
  1-cohomology \(H^1 \ne 0\) and circulation around holes cannot be
  reached from 0-cochain boundaries (\(B^1 = \mathrm{im}(d_0)\)).
  Coboundaries strictly vanish on cycles
  (\texttt{n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}y}).
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{Rung 3: Weights to Probabilities
(\(L^1 \to L^2\) \& Born
Normalization)}{Rung 3: Weights to Probabilities (L\^{}1 \textbackslash to L\^{}2 \& Born Normalization)}}\label{rung-3-weights-to-probabilities-l1-to-l2-born-normalization}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?} \(L^1\) normalization of positive
  residual weights into probability distributions
  \(p_i = w_i / \sum w_k\), ray invariance under positive scaling
  \(w \mapsto c w\) (\(c > 0\)), rank-1 projector construction
  \(P = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) with idempotence \(P^2 = P\) and
  self-adjointness \(P^\dagger = P\), and the algebraic redundancy
  theorem showing that for any complete POVM partition of identity
  \(\sum_k E_k = I\), the outcome probabilities satisfy
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \sum_k \operatorname{Tr}(E_k \rho) = \operatorname{Tr}((\sum_k E_k)\rho) = \operatorname{Tr}(I \rho) = \operatorname{Tr}(\rho) = 1\)}\].
  The general trace identity is the displayed linear-algebra argument.
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}B\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}N\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  mechanizes a two-level diagonal model with natural-number effect
  coefficients and scaled integer rank-one matrices
  (\texttt{b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}y},
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t},
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e},

\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The
  quadratic Born rule mapping state amplitudes to detection
  probabilities (\(p_i = |\psi_i|^2\)). It is imported as a declared
  postulate/contract; it is not derived from \(L^1\) weights.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?} The \(L^1\)
  simplex alone does not select the quadratic Born readout. A Gleason or
  Busch route adds explicit projection/effect-domain, positivity and
  additivity premises. Projective Gleason uniqueness fails in dimension
  two; stronger all-effects assumptions allow a different representation
  route even there. Neither route derives its operational domain from
  primitive difference.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Rung 4: Phase, Interference \& Superposition as Quotient
Fiber}\label{rung-4-phase-interference-superposition-as-quotient-fiber}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What follows under the declared complex carrier?} The
  \(U(1)\) phase fiber \(e^{i \theta}\), holonomy around closed cycles
  in the complex, and superposition as the fiber over the classical
  probability simplex. Standard projectivization is
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \mathbb P(\mathcal H)=(\mathcal H\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times
  \cong S(\mathcal H)/U(1)\)}\], where \(S(\mathcal H)\) is the unit
  sphere. This is distinct from the group quotient
  \(\mathbb C^\times/U(1)\), which retains only positive scale. The
  basis-dependent projection
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle [\psi] \mapsto (|\psi_i|^2 / \|\psi\|^2)_{i=1}^d \in \Delta^{d-1}\)}\],
  whose fiber over an outcome distribution with \(k\) nonzero components
  is the torus \(T^{k-1}\) parameterized by \(k-1\) relative phases that
  govern interference capacity (the largest constructive cross term is
  \(2 \sum_{j < k} |\psi_j| |\psi_k|\)), real two-state interference
  with cross-term \(2 c_0 c_1\), and Sorkin's {[}7{]} third-order term
  \(I_3(A,B,C)=0\) for a quadratic readout; the second-order term can be
  nonzero. The torus description is the usual complex-coordinate
  argument: fix the nonzero moduli and quotient the \(k\) independent
  phases by their common phase.
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  establishes integer two-state and integer polynomial identities
  (\texttt{s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e});
  it does not construct that complex torus. Numerical examples are

  (\texttt{s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t},
  \texttt{t\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}3\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r}).
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The
  complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) and the circle group \(U(1)\) as the
  phase fiber.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?} The
  continuous circle group \(U(1)\) and phase interference are not
  supplied by the stated classical stochastic or \(L^1\) transport

\paragraph{Rung 5: Composition, Entanglement \&
Non-Separability}\label{rung-5-composition-entanglement-non-separability}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What follows under the declared tensor carrier?} The
  standard Schmidt decomposition characterizes pure-state entanglement
  by Schmidt rank greater than one. On the supplied carrier
  \(\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B\), we check the 2x2 Schmidt minor
  condition
  (\[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \Delta(\psi) = c_{00} c_{11} - c_{01} c_{10} = 0\)}\]
  for all separable product states), and non-product certification of
  the Bell state
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |\Phi^+\rangle=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2\)}\]
  (\(\Delta=1/2\); its unnormalized integer representative has
  \(\Delta=1\)), partial trace
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B(\rho_{AB})\)}\],
  linear and von Neumann entanglement entropies, the non-signaling
  theorem under local operations on subsystem B
  (\[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Tr}_B((I_A \otimes U_B)\rho_{AB}(I_A \otimes U_B^\dagger)) = \operatorname{Tr}_B(\rho_{AB})\)}\]),
  and the Mermin--Peres contextuality parity obstruction. The
  partial-trace identity follows by cyclicity on the traced factor and
  \(U_B^\dagger U_B=I\). Lean coverage is narrower: the parity argument
  is mechanized in
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}W\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  (\texttt{m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n}),
  \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}E\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  uses integer \(2\times2\) coefficients for the minor and establishes
  marginal invariance for a local bit flip and sign change
  (\texttt{p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d},
  \texttt{n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}p},
  \texttt{n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e})
  and computed in
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
  (\texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y},
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e},
  \texttt{v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g},
  \texttt{i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e}).
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The
  Hilbert space tensor product \(\otimes\) as the composition rule. The
  finite tests check bilinearity, local unitary covariance,
  product-state marginal consistency and no-signalling, and exclude one
  report-discarding rival. It does not prove uniqueness among all
  composites. A generation, local-tomography or minimality premise must
  exclude additional invisible sectors before such a classification.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What remains an additional premise?} A single-carrier
  cochain construction supplies no bipartite composition law. Under
  ordinary classical Cartesian composition every joint distribution is a
  mixture of point products (§11.33 above). Quantum tensor composition
  permits nonseparable states; the Mermin--Peres experiment excludes its
  specified noncontextual assignments. Contextuality by itself neither
  requires this tensor presentation nor selects complex quantum theory
  among all operational models.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Rung 6: Dynamics (Discrete Unitary
Evolution)}\label{rung-6-dynamics-discrete-unitary-evolution}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?} Discrete unitary operators
  \(U^\dagger U = I\), discrete state evolution
  \(\psi(t+1) = U \psi(t)\) and \(\rho(t+1) = U \rho(t) U^\dagger\), and
  conservation of \(L^2\) state norm \(\|\psi\|_2 = 1\). Computed in
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}.
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The
  requirement of reversibility\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}unitarity and a
  discrete time step parameter.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?} Continuous
  time and self-adjoint Hamiltonian generators \(H\) via Stone's theorem
  (\(U(t) = \exp(-i H t)\)) cannot be reached from discrete dynamics.
  Discrete toggles (e.g.~Pauli X) have infinitely many matrix logarithms
  (branch ambiguities), so continuous time remains a declared
  hypothesis.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Rung 7: Measurement \& Open Systems (Effects, POVMs,
CPTP)}\label{rung-7-measurement-open-systems-effects-povms-cptp}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?} Positive Operator-Valued Measure
  (POVM) effects \(E_m \ge 0\), \(\sum E_m = I\), Born rule outcome
  probabilities
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle P(m) = \operatorname{Tr}(E_m \rho)\)}\],
  Lüders state update and non-selective measurement decoherence
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \rho \mapsto \sum M_m \rho M_m^\dagger\)}\],
  and trace-norm contractivity under CPTP maps. These are consequences
  of the imported quantum definitions. The cited
  \texttt{F\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  theorem
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l}
  establishes only the bound for a two-entry diagonal rational spectrum
  and binary diagonal projective effects; it is not a proof of general
  CPTP contractivity.
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
  supplies numerical examples; §§11.35--11.38 above give the exact
  finite checks.
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The POVM
  effect algebra and the definition of completely positive
  trace-preserving (CPTP) maps, defined via Choi positivity in the
  declared embedding and exact trace preservation. A chosen spectral
  Kraus construction can require square roots outside the base field;
  this is not a channel-wide obstruction. The native
  rational\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}Gaussian-rational LDL* construction
  can split positive rational pivots into four squares and enlarge the
  Kraus family without adjoining those square roots (see the channel
  census below).
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?}
  Non-selective measurement\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}dephasing channels
  admit finite-dimensional Stinespring dilations (e.g.~coupling to a
  single ancilla qubit via CNOT followed by partial trace), but
  selective projective collapse to a single measurement branch is
  non-unitary and irreversible. Unitary coupling and a discarded
  environment can produce the non-selective reduced channel, but do not
  select one realized branch. Conditional updating presupposes a
  recorded outcome; an account of its occurrence needs an additional
  stated premise: this is the unresolved quantum measurement problem.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Rung 8: The Boundary \& Gleason's Theorem
Obstruction}\label{rung-8-the-boundary-gleasons-theorem-obstruction}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{(i) What is derived here?}
  \texttt{G\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  formalizes integer quadratic frame identities and an odd-integer
  obstruction, not a general Gleason theorem.
  \texttt{G\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}R\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  now constructs a binary function on every nonzero rational two-vector,
  verifies invariance under nonzero rational rescaling and normalization
  on every orthogonal pair, and rules out a rational quadratic
  representation using four rays.
  \texttt{H\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}5\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}O\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  establishes the nine-context Cabello parity contradiction {[}2{]} and
  checks that a trace-one non-PSD matrix passes all 18 sampled ray
  bounds and nine frame sums.
  \texttt{H\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}5\allowbreak{}8\allowbreak{}E\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}B\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
  formalizes four-effect tomographic uniqueness and recovery on a
  supplied two-dimensional Hermitian coordinate space. Its
  rational-homogeneity result assumes an explicit homogeneity witness;
  its three-dimensional uniqueness result assumes the needed coordinate
  equations. The repaired three-dimensional effect predicate checks all
  principal minors, including the determinant. These declarations are
  not Busch's full positive representation theorem {[}3{]}. The Rust
  \texttt{F\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}f}
  now enforces that separation with the linear-algebra owner's exact
  inertia checker.
\item
  \textbf{(ii) What is imported here, and named as an import?} The full
  Gleason theorem in dimension \(d \ge 3\) (showing that normalization
  and additivity across every orthonormal basis of the full real or
  complex Hilbert space force nonnegative frame functions to be
  quadratic Born valuations \(f(v) = v^\dagger \rho v\)) is a classical
  continuum theorem on complete projective geometries. Applying it to a
  restricted number-field ray domain requires an additional extension
  theorem; neither countability nor a finite test configuration
  demonstrates such an extension or the necessity of a continuum
  completion.
\item
  \textbf{(iii) What cannot be reached from below, and why?} Continuous
  canonical observables \([X, P] = i\hbar I\) cannot be reached in any
  finite dimension (trace obstruction:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Tr}([X, P]) = 0 \ne i\hbar d\)}\]).
  This is the finite-dimensional trace obstruction; Wintner--Wielandt is
  the stronger bounded-operator obstruction. Constructing an
  infinite-dimensional Hilbert completion additionally requires a
  directed family, inner products and a topology. None is supplied by a
  finite graph alone.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{1.2 The 22 Foundational Targets (Loops 1 to
22)}\label{the-22-foundational-targets-loops-1-to-22}

To test the finite quantum mechanics programme against concrete physical
and computational structures, 22 Foundational Targets (organized across
Loops 1 to 22) specify finite models and examples. Their mathematical
specifications, numerical Python demonstrations, exact native checks and
scoped Lean declarations are different evidence. The list is not a
certificate that every named target or general theorem has been
implemented. The declared algebraic carriers include the rationals
\(\mathbb{Q}\), Gaussian integers \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\), Eisenstein
rationals \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)\), cyclotomic rings
\[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_5], \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_8], \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{12}]\)}\],
quadratic fields
\[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3}), \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{N})\)}\],
finite fields \(\mathbb{F}_p\), and cyclic groups
\(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\).

\paragraph{Detailed Mathematical Specifications for Targets 13 through
22 (Loops 13 to
22)}\label{detailed-mathematical-specifications-for-targets-13-through-22-loops-13-to-22}

\subparagraph{\texorpdfstring{Target 13 (Loop 13): Prime-\(p\) Discrete
Wigner Phase Space
(\(p=5\))}{Target 13 (Loop 13): Prime-p Discrete Wigner Phase Space (p=5)}}\label{target-13-loop-13-prime-p-discrete-wigner-phase-space-p5}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} On a discrete phase
  space \(\mathbb{F}_p \times \mathbb{F}_p\) for an odd prime \(p=5\),
  the finite Weyl-Heisenberg group {[}4{]} is generated by the cyclic
  coordinate shift operator
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle X |k\rangle = |k + 1 \pmod p\rangle\)}\]
  and clock operator \(Z |k\rangle = \omega^k |k\rangle\), where
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \omega = \zeta_p = \exp(2\pi i / p)\)}\].
  The parity reflection operator is defined on basis states by
  \(P |k\rangle = |-k \pmod p\rangle\), which acts on integer coordinate
  vectors
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle (v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4)^T \in \mathbb{Z}^5\)}\]
  via
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle P (v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4)^T = (v_0, v_4, v_3, v_2, v_1)^T.\)}\]
  Writing phase-space coordinates as \((q,r)\) to distinguish them from
  the prime dimension \(p\), the symmetric Weyl displacement convention
  is
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle D(q, r) = \omega^{2^{-1} q r \pmod p} X^q Z^r,\)}\]
  where
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle 2^{-1} \equiv \frac{p+1}{2} \equiv 3 \pmod 5\)}\].
  The Gross discrete phase-point operators are constructed as displaced
  parity reflections:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle A(q, r) = D(q, r) P D(q, r)^\dagger.\)}\]
  This positive displacement exponent matches \(ZX=\omega XZ\); scalar
  phase changes in \(D\) cancel in \(A\). The discrete Wigner function
  for a state \(\rho\) is then
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle W_\rho(q, r) = \frac{1}{p} \operatorname{Tr}(\rho A(q, r))\)}\].
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} Exact cyclotomic field
  \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)\) with minimal polynomial
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \Phi_5(x) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0\)}\],
  ring of integers \(\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_5]\), discrete field
  \(\mathbb{F}_5\), and coordinate lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^5\).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Involution: \(P^2 = I_5\).
  \item
    Hermiticity: \(A(u)^\dagger = A(u)\) for all
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle u = (q, r) \in \mathbb{F}_5 \times \mathbb{F}_5\)}\].
  \item
    Trace normalization: \(\operatorname{Tr}(A(u)) = 1\).
  \item
    Phase-point orthogonality:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Tr}(A(u) A(v)) = 5 \, \delta_{u, v}\)}\].
  \item
    Completeness:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \sum_{u \in \mathbb{F}_5 \times \mathbb{F}_5} A(u) = 5 \, I_5\)}\].
  \item
    Gross stabilizer covariance: \(P X P = X^{-1}\) and
    \(U_S A(u) U_S^\dagger = A(S u)\) for all
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle S \in \operatorname{Sp}(2, \mathbb{F}_5)\)}\].
  \item
    Stabilizer non-negativity: the stabilizer eigenstates \(|0\rangle\)
    and
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \sum_k |k\rangle\)}\]
    satisfy \(P |0\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(P |+\rangle = |+\rangle\),
    yielding non-negative Wigner values
    (\(W_{|0\rangle}(0, 0) = 1/5 > 0\)).
  \item
    Point negativity witness: the non-stabilizer vector
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |M\rangle = (0, 1, 0, 0, -1)^T \in \mathbb{Z}^5\)}\]
    satisfies \(P|M\rangle=-|M\rangle\), yielding
    \(\langle M|P|M\rangle=-2\). Its normalized projector
    \(|M\rangle\langle M|/2\) has Wigner value \(-1/5\) at the origin.
    The projector remains in the stated field even when a normalized
    vector requires an extension.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
    (\texttt{b\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}s},
    \texttt{e\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r},
    \texttt{v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e}).
    The phase-point builder and Fourier\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}shear
    covariance checks are floating-point diagnostics restricted to the
    paper's \(p=3,5\) fixtures. Their measured residuals use the stated
    absolute tolerance \(10^{-10}\) and are not exact algebraic
    certificates. The odd-prime algebraic construction is separate from
    this numerical replay.
  \item

    supplies exact phase-point operators, using
    \texttt{o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g}
    and

\subparagraph{Target 14 (Loop 14): Shor {[}{[}9, 1, 3{]}{]} Concatenated
Quantum Error Correcting
Code}\label{target-14-loop-14-shor-9-1-3-concatenated-quantum-error-correcting-code}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} The Shor code
  concatenates a 3-qubit phase-flip repetition code with an inner
  3-qubit bit-flip code, encoding \(k=1\) logical qubit into \(n=9\)
  physical qubits. The code space is the \(+1\) eigenspace of 8
  independent commuting stabilizer generators:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Six local \(Z\)-type stabilizer checks, which detect bit-flip
    (\(X\)) errors:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle S_1 = Z_0 Z_1, \quad S_2 = Z_1 Z_2, \quad S_3 = Z_3 Z_4, \quad S_4 = Z_4 Z_5, \quad S_5 = Z_6 Z_7, \quad S_6 = Z_7 Z_8.\)}\]
    For example, \(\{Z_0 Z_1, X_0\} = 0\) while \([Z_0 Z_1, Z_0] = 0\).
  \item
    Two global \(X\)-type stabilizer checks, which detect phase-flip
    (\(Z\)) errors:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle S_7 = X_0 X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4 X_5, \quad S_8 = X_3 X_4 X_5 X_6 X_7 X_8.\)}\]
    For example, \(\{S_7, Z_0\} = 0\) while \([S_7, X_0] = 0\). The
    logical operators are given by:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle X_L = \bigotimes_{j=0}^8 X_j \quad (\text{weight } 9), \qquad Z_L = Z_0 Z_3 Z_6 \quad (\text{weight } 3).\)}\]
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} 9-qubit tensor space
  \((\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes 9}\) restricted to exact integer Pauli
  matrices over \(\mathbb{Z}\), binary syndrome space
  \(\mathbb{F}_2^8\).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Pairwise stabilizer commutation: \([S_i, S_j] = 0\) for all
    \(i, j \in \{1, \dots, 8\}\).
  \item
    Logical-stabilizer commutation: \([X_L, S_i] = 0\) and
    \([Z_L, S_i] = 0\) for all \(i\).
  \item
    Logical anticommutation: \(\{X_L, Z_L\} = 0\) via symplectic inner
    product \((-1)^3 = -1\).
  \item
    Code distance \(d = 3\): the minimum weight of an undetectable
    logical operator in \(N(S) \setminus S\) is 3.
  \item
    Syndrome decoding completeness: all 27 single-qubit Pauli errors
    \(\{X_i, Y_i, Z_i\}_{i=0}^8\) produce non-zero 8-bit syndrome
    vectors \(s(E) \in \mathbb{F}_2^8\) with \(s_j(E) = 0\) if
    \([E, S_j] = 0\) and \(1\) if \(\{E, S_j\} = 0\).
  \item
    Recovery fidelity: minimum-weight syndrome lookup yields exact
    recovery fidelity \(F = 1.0\) across all 27 single-qubit error
    channels.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
    (\texttt{b\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e},

\subparagraph{Target 15 (Loop 15): Discrete Quantum Phase Estimation
over Cyclotomic
Ring}\label{target-15-loop-15-discrete-quantum-phase-estimation-over-cyclotomic-ring}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} Discrete Phase
  Estimation measures the eigenphase \(\theta \in [0, 1)\) of a unitary
  operator \(U\) satisfying
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle U |\psi\rangle = e^{2\pi i \theta} |\psi\rangle\)}\].
  When \(\theta\) is a dyadic rational \(\theta = k / 2^m\) for
  \(k \in \{0, \dots, 2^m - 1\}\), the register state before the inverse
  quantum Fourier transform is
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |\Psi_k\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^m}} \sum_{l=0}^{2^m - 1} e^{2\pi i \theta l} |l\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^m}} \sum_{l=0}^{2^m - 1} \zeta_{2^m}^{k l} |l\rangle.\)}\]
  For \(m=2\) (\(M=4\) register levels),
  \(\zeta_4 = i \in \mathbb{Z}[i]\). The unnormalized inverse discrete
  Fourier transform operator \(F_4^\dagger\) has matrix entries:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle (F_4^\dagger)_{j, l} = (-i)^{j \cdot l} \in \mathbb{Z}[i].\)}\]
  Applying \(F_4^\dagger\) to \(|\Psi_k\rangle\) yields the
  transformation:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle (F_4^\dagger |\Psi_k\rangle)_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \sum_{l=0}^3 (-i)^{j l} i^{k l} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l=0}^3 i^{(k - j) l}.\)}\]
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} Gaussian integers
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \mathbb{Z}[i] = \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_4]\)}\]
  with minimal polynomial \(x^2 + 1 = 0\), dyadic rational field
  \(\mathbb{Q}\), integer coordinate vectors \(\mathbb{Z}^4\).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Destructive interference: for all false bins \(j \ne k \pmod 4\),
    the geometric series evaluates to
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \sum_{l=0}^3 i^{(k - j) l} = \frac{1 - i^{4(k - j)}}{1 - i^{k - j}} = \frac{1 - 1}{1 - i^{k - j}} = 0.\)}\]
  \item
    Constructive reinforcement: for the true bin \(j = k\), each term is
    \(i^0 = 1\), yielding
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \sum_{l=0}^3 1 = 4.\)}\]
  \item
    Deterministic projection:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^m}} F_4^\dagger |\Psi_k\rangle = |k\rangle\)}\]
    (or unnormalized
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle F_4^\dagger |\Psi_k\rangle = 2 |k\rangle\)}\]),
    establishing exact dyadic phase extraction with zero phase leakage.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
    (\texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}t},
    \texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n},
    \texttt{v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n}).
  \item
    Lean 4:
    \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}H\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}3\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}E\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
    (\texttt{p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}0},
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}0},
    \texttt{z\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s},
    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n},
    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t},
    \texttt{d\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}s}).
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subparagraph{Target 16 (Loop 16): Surface Code Toric Topology \& Anyon
Defect
Algebra}\label{target-16-loop-16-surface-code-toric-topology-anyon-defect-algebra}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} On a 2-dimensional
  periodic lattice representing the torus \(T^2\) with \(V=4\) vertices,
  \(E=8\) edges, and \(P=4\) plaquettes, Kitaev's toric code is defined
  by:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Star operators:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle A_s = \prod_{e \in \operatorname{star}(s)} X_e\)}\]
    for each vertex \(s\).
  \item
    Plaquette operators:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle B_p = \prod_{e \in \partial p} Z_e\)}\]
    for each face \(p\). The lattice geometry satisfies the Euler
    characteristic relation:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \chi = V - E + P = 4 - 8 + 4 = 0 \implies g = 1 - \chi / 2 = 1.\)}\]
    The first homology group over \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) has dimension
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle b_1 = \dim H_1(T^2, \mathbb{Z}_2) = 2\)}\],
    encoding \(k = b_1 = 2\) logical qubits into \(n = 8\) physical edge
    qubits.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} Cellular chain complex
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle C_2 \xrightarrow{\partial_2} C_1 \xrightarrow{\partial_1} C_0\)}\]
  over \(\mathbb{Z}_2\), integer Pauli group on 8 qubits, Abelian anyon
  defect algebra (mutual braiding phase \(-1\)).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Star-plaquette commutation: each star and plaquette share an even
    number of edges (\(|s \cap p| \in \{0, 2\}\)), ensuring
    \([A_s, B_p] = 0\) via \((-1)^0 = (-1)^2 = +1\) across all 16 pairs.
  \item
    Ground state degeneracy: the number of independent checks is
    \((V - 1) + (P - 1) = 3 + 3 = 6\), leaving \(8 - 6 = 2\) logical
    qubits and a 4-fold degenerate ground state space
    \(\mathcal{H}_{\text{code}}\).
  \item
    Anyon defect pairs: an open \(Z\)-string creates two electric
    (\(e\)) defects at star endpoints (\(A_s = -1\)), while an open
    \(X\)-string creates two magnetic flux (\(m\)) defects at plaquette
    endpoints (\(B_p = -1\)).
  \item
    Abelian mutual braiding phase: a closed \(e\)-loop encircling a
    single \(m\)-defect intersects the dual \(m\)-string at an odd
    number of edges (exactly 1 edge in the minimal cell), resulting in
    the topological braiding phase factor \((-1)^1 = -1 = e^{i\pi}\).
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}

\subparagraph{Target 17 (Loop 17): Discrete Grover Search via
Householder
Reflections}\label{target-17-loop-17-discrete-grover-search-via-householder-reflections}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} Discrete Grover
  search on an unstructured database of size \(N=4\) operates in a
  2-dimensional invariant subspace spanned by the marked target state
  \(|\omega\rangle\) and the uniform superposition
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{x=0}^{N-1} |x\rangle\)}\].
  The Grover iteration is \(G = D R_\omega\), where:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Oracle reflection:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle R_\omega = I - 2 |\omega\rangle\langle\omega|\)}\].
  \item
    Householder diffusion reflection: \(D = 2 |s\rangle\langle s| - I\).
    Scaled by 2 to clear denominators, the diffusion operator is
    \(\widetilde{D} = J_4 - 2 I_4\), where \(J_4\) is the all-ones
    matrix. The initial overlap angle \(\theta\) satisfies
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} = \frac{1}{2}\)}\],
    giving \(\theta = \pi/6\) and Grover step rotation angle
    \(2\theta = \pi/3\).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} Quadratic ring \(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{3}]\)
  with \((a + b\sqrt{3})\), rational field \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{N})\), and
  integer matrix ring \(M_4(\mathbb{Z})\).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Diffusion involution:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \widetilde{D}^2 = (J_4 - 2 I_4)^2 = J_4^2 - 4 J_4 + 4 I_4 = 4 J_4 - 4 J_4 + 4 I_4 = 4 I_4\)}\].
  \item
    Exact 1-step target concentration: for initial state
    \(|s\rangle = (1, 1, 1, 1)^T\) and target
    \(|\omega\rangle = (1, 0, 0, 0)^T\), applying the oracle and scaled
    diffusion yields
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \widetilde{D} R_0 |s\rangle = (J_4 - 2 I_4) (-1, 1, 1, 1)^T = (4, 0, 0, 0)^T = 4 |\omega\rangle,\)}\]
    recovering the target state with 100\% fidelity in a single discrete
    step.
  \item
    Discrete Chebyshev recurrence: the target amplitude sequence
    \(s_k = \sin((2k+1)\theta)\) satisfies the linear difference
    equation \(s_{k+1} = s_k - s_{k-1}\) over \(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{3}]\),
    producing the exact periodic sequence
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle (1/2, 1, 1/2, -1/2, -1, -1/2, \dots)\)}\]
    with period 6.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
    (\texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}p},
    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t},
    \texttt{v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}p}).
  \item

    (\texttt{d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d},
    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t},
    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n},

    \texttt{g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}x}).

\subparagraph{Target 18 (Loop 18): Discrete Clifford Group Structure \&
Eastin-Knill
Limit}\label{target-18-loop-18-discrete-clifford-group-structure-eastin-knill-limit}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} The \(n\)-qubit
  Clifford group \(C_n\) is the normalizer of the Pauli group \(P_n\) in
  \(\operatorname{U}(2^n)\). After dividing out all scalar phases, write
  \(\overline C_n\) and \(\overline P_n\) for the projective groups. The
  quotient \(\overline C_n/\overline P_n\) is isomorphic to the finite
  symplectic group
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb F_2)\)}\]
  preserving the symplectic bilinear form
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \omega(u, v) = u_x v_z + u_z v_x \pmod 2.\)}\]
  For a single qubit (\(n=1\)),
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Sp}(2, \mathbb{F}_2) = \operatorname{SL}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)\)}\],
  consisting of \(2 \times 2\) binary matrices with determinant
  \(1 \pmod 2\). The group is generated by the symplectic images of the
  Hadamard gate \(H\) and Phase gate \(S\):
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle H = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\)}\]
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} Finite field \(\mathbb{F}_2\), symplectic
  space \(\mathbb{F}_2^2\), permutation group \(S_3\).
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Symplectic group order formula:
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle |\operatorname{Sp}(2n, \mathbb{F}_2)| = 2^{n^2} \prod_{j=1}^n (2^{2j} - 1) \implies |\operatorname{Sp}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)| = 2^1 (2^2 - 1) = 6.\)}\]
  \item
    Isomorphism to \(S_3\): the 6 matrices partition into:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Identity: \(I\) (order 1).
    \item
      Three order-2 involutions: \(H, S, HSH\) (satisfying \(M^2 = I\)).
    \item
      Two order-3 rotations: \(SH, HS\) (satisfying \(M^3 = I\)).
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Symplectic invariance: \(\omega(M u, M v) = \omega(u, v)\) for all
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle M \in \operatorname{Sp}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)\)}\]
    and all \(u, v \in \mathbb{F}_2^2\).
  \item
    Symplectic quotient closure and Eastin-Knill transversal
    restriction: the single-qubit projective Clifford group quotient
    \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \mathcal{C}_1 / \mathcal{P}_1 \cong \operatorname{Sp}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)\)}\]
    has finite order 6 (projective Clifford order 24), closed under
    multiplication. Their finiteness precludes a dense projective gate
    set generated by those elements alone. A separate imported theorem
    of Eastin and Knill {[}25{]} states that a quantum error-correcting
    code detecting arbitrary errors on any single physical subsystem, in
    the stated finite-dimensional setting, admits no transversal encoded
    gate set that generates a dense subgroup of the encoded unitary
    group. The finite group checks here do not prove that general
    theorem or classify every transversal encoded operation of an
    arbitrary code.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Python:
    \texttt{p\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}y}
    (\texttt{c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r},
    \texttt{b\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s},
    \texttt{v\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}1},
    \texttt{e\allowbreak{}v\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n}).
  \item
    Lean 4:
    \texttt{l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}H\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n}
    (\texttt{s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y},

\subparagraph{Target 19 (Loop 19): The Finite CCR Trace Obstruction and
the Weyl
Representation}\label{target-19-loop-19-the-finite-ccr-trace-obstruction-and-the-weyl-representation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical Specification \& Operators:} In continuous
  quantum mechanics, the canonical commutation relation
  \([Q, P] = i \hbar I\) governs conjugate position and momentum
  observables. On a finite-dimensional carrier \(\mathbb{C}^N\) (or
  cyclic coordinate space \(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\)), the trace of any
  matrix commutator \([Q, P] = Q P - P Q\) satisfies the algebraic
  identity:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle \operatorname{Tr}([Q, P]) = \operatorname{Tr}(QP) - \operatorname{Tr}(PQ) = 0.\)}\]
  Taking the trace of the canonical relation yields the obstruction:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle 0 = \operatorname{Tr}([Q, P]) \ne \operatorname{Tr}(i \hbar I_N) = i \hbar N \quad (\text{for } N \ge 1, \hbar \ne 0).\)}\]
  This trace argument excludes the additive canonical commutation
  relation in finite dimension over characteristic zero. It is not the
  Stone--von Neumann uniqueness theorem, and the obstruction concerns
  dimension rather than the cardinality of scalar coordinates. The
  finite presentation circumvents this obstruction via the discrete
  Weyl-Heisenberg shift \(X\) and clock \(Z\):
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle X |k\rangle = |k + 1 \pmod N\rangle, \qquad Z |k\rangle = \omega^k |k\rangle, \quad \omega = e^{2\pi i / N},\)}\]
  which satisfy the discrete Weyl commutation relation:
  \[\protect\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{\(\displaystyle Z X = \omega X Z \iff X^a Z^b = \omega^{-ab} Z^b X^a.\)}\]
\item
  \textbf{Discrete Carrier:} The cyclic label set is
  \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). The shift is integral, but the clock needs a
  scalar field containing a primitive \(N\)th root of unity, for example
  \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_N)\) with its declared complex embedding. Unitary
  equivalence may require normalization scalars beyond that field.
\item
  \textbf{Invariants \& Algebraic Relations:}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Vanishing trace identity: \(\operatorname{Tr}([A, B]) = 0\) holds
    identically for all finite matrices over any commutative ring.
  \item
    Multiplicative Weyl relation: \([X,Z]=(1-\omega)XZ\) has trace zero
    since \(\operatorname{Tr}(XZ)=0\) for \(N\ge2\). This commutator is
    generally not central; it does not assert the additive CCR, which
    has no finite-dimensional solution (trace argument).
  \item
    Under a fixed nondegenerate multiplier (primitive \(\omega\)), the
    standard finite Stone--von Neumann theorem over \(\mathbb C\) gives
    the irreducible representation up to unitary equivalence. Our exact
    construction has the more explicit supplied-seed premises below; it
    does not find or normalize an eigenvector over every input number
    field.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Cross-References:}
